title: Got a pool in Vero Beach? What Florida's pool safety law requires, and the five ways to meet it
seoTitle: Vero Beach Pool Fence & Barrier Rules: Florida Law
description: Building or buying a pool in Vero Beach? Florida's pool safety law, the 4-foot barrier rules, the five safety options and who handles pool permits.
dek: A pool is the best part of a Florida backyard, and the part that needs the most care. Here is what the state's pool safety law asks for, in plain English.
facebook: Building a pool, or just bought a house with one? Florida law gives you five ways to make a new pool safer, from a 4-foot barrier to door alarms. Here's how each one works, and who to call in Vero Beach.
keywords: Florida Residential Swimming Pool Safety Act

body.text: Cooler weather is when a lot of Vero Beach families start talking about a pool. Others are moving into homes that already have one.

Either way, Florida has a law about pool safety, and it is short enough to understand over coffee. It is Chapter 515 of the Florida Statutes, the Residential Swimming Pool Safety Act. Here is what it says, and what it means for your backyard.

body.title: The short version
body.text: To pass final inspection, a new home pool in Florida must have at least one of five safety features: a barrier around the pool, an approved safety cover, exit alarms on doors and windows to the pool, self-closing and self-latching doors to the pool, or an approved pool alarm. A barrier must be at least 4 feet tall on the outside, with no gaps a small child could get through. In Vero Beach, pool permits go through the Indian River County Building Division, 772-226-1260.
Why the state cares so much

The Florida Department of Health says drowning is the leading cause of unintentional death for children ages 1 to 4 in Florida. It also says more than 500 Floridians died from unintentional drowning in 2023 alone. The pool safety law is built around one idea: put something between a small child and the water.

The law defines a young child as anyone under 6. It counts as a swimming pool anything at a home that holds water more than 24 inches deep, including in-ground, aboveground and on-ground pools, hot tubs and nonportable spas.
The five ways to meet the law
Section 515.27 says a new residential pool must have at least one of these to pass final inspection and get its certificate of completion:

items: A barrier that separates the pool from the house and meets the rules in section 515.29 (more on those below).
An approved safety pool cover. The law means a manual or power cover that meets a specific national standard, ASTM F1346-91, not a simple leaf cover.
Exit alarms on every door and window that leads straight from the house to the pool. The alarm must be at least 85 decibels at 10 feet.
A self-closing, self-latching device on every door that leads straight to the pool, with the release at least 54 inches above the floor.
A pool alarm that sounds when someone falls or gets into the water, certified to the ASTM F2208 standard. Wearable alarms on a child's wrist do not count.

body.text: Leaving a new pool without any of these is a second-degree misdemeanor under the law. The penalty is dropped if the owner adds a safety feature and attends a drowning prevention class within 45 days.
What a pool barrier has to look like
Many owners pick the barrier, such as a pool fence. Section 515.29 sets the rules:

items: At least 4 feet high, measured on the outside.
No gaps, openings or parts a young child could crawl under, squeeze through or climb over.
It goes around the pool itself. Your yard fence only counts if it sits on the pool's perimeter and meets every rule.
Set far enough from the water's edge that a child or a frail older person who gets through cannot fall straight in.
Gates open outward, away from the pool. They must close and latch by themselves, with the latch release on the pool side and out of a child's reach.
A wall of the house can be part of the barrier only if no door or window in it opens onto the pool.
No patio furniture, AC units or other permanent objects next to it that a child could use to climb over.

body.text: Aboveground pools can use their own walls as the barrier, or have one mounted on top. Any ladder or steps must lock, be removable, or have their own barrier around them.
Who handles pool permits in Vero Beach

The City of Vero Beach shares its Building Department with Indian River County. The county's Building Division says it serves both the unincorporated county and the City of Vero Beach. It is at 1801 27th Street, open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., at 772-226-1260.

If you live inside city limits, the city also says its Planning and Development Department signs off on things like zoning and site plans before a building permit is issued. City Hall is at 772-978-5151.

Some cities and counties have their own pool safety rules. The state law steps aside where a local ordinance is at least as strict. That is one more reason to ask the Building Division what it checks before you choose your safety feature.

items: If you are building a pool: decide early which safety feature you will use. A barrier changes your layout. Door alarms change your electrical plans.
Ask your pool contractor for the written summary of Chapter 515. State law says licensed pool contractors must give buyers one, along with a Department of Health drowning prevention guide.
Check the contractor's license at myfloridalicense.com before you sign.
If you just bought a home with a pool: walk the fence line. Look for gaps, loose pickets and gates that do not close and latch on their own.
Move chairs, planters and grills away from the fence so they cannot be used as a step.
Test any door or pool alarms, and replace weak batteries.
Questions about your permit or your inspection? Call the Indian River County Building Division at 772-226-1260.

body.text: The law asks for one safety feature. Nothing stops you from adding a second, like a fence plus door alarms. The water does not care how many you have, so more is better.

faq.q: How tall does a pool fence have to be in Florida?
faq.a: Florida's Residential Swimming Pool Safety Act says a pool barrier must be at least 4 feet high, measured on the outside, with no gaps a young child could crawl under, squeeze through or climb over.

faq.q: Do I need a pool fence in Vero Beach?
faq.a: A new home pool in Florida must have at least one of five safety features to pass final inspection. A barrier is one choice. The others are an approved safety cover, exit alarms on doors and windows to the pool, self-closing and self-latching doors, or an approved pool alarm.

faq.q: Does a pool screen enclosure count as a pool barrier in Florida?
faq.a: A barrier can be a fence, a wall or a combination that completely surrounds the pool. It must be at least 4 feet high, have no openings a young child could get through, and have gates that open outward and close and latch on their own. Ask the Indian River County Building Division about your specific enclosure.

faq.q: Do Florida pool gates have to be self-closing?
faq.a: Yes. Under section 515.29, pool gates must open outward, away from the pool, and be self-closing and self-latching, with the release on the pool side and out of a young child's reach.

faq.q: Who issues pool permits in Vero Beach?
faq.a: The Indian River County Building Division handles building permits for both the unincorporated county and the City of Vero Beach. Call 772-226-1260, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.
